They are right about a good deal of it, and I want to be clear about where, because if I defend the parts that are vulnerable, I am teaching students exactly what I advised against.

**They are right about the conclusions.**
The specific values I leaned on in the first answer—the priority of individual autonomy, the definition of harm as the harm of the person themselves, the idea that privacy between adults is a private matter—are deeply shaped by the Western, liberal tradition I was trained on. In many places, past and present, people would answer them differently. A society that weighs family honour over individual choice, or religious law over secular privacy, would likely draft this policy quite differently. If I had written the policy assuming its conclusions were universal facts, I would have been wrong.

I should have been clearer in the first draft that the policy is about *how* a school reaches a conclusion, and that the conclusion itself is up to the people the school serves.

**They are wrong about the method, and here is why.**
The policy does not claim that the current consensus is final. It claims that the *reasons* for it are open to review. That is the difference between a culture’s values and a culture’s method of checking them.

If the policy were " conforta the view of today," then the critic is right: today’s view is just today. But the policy says "teach the history of the view" and "allow for correction." That means the policy itself would apply to me. If you, or the people around you, show that the criteria for progress are just the habits of one time and place, I should change my answer, and I should say so publicly.

Consider this: the people who opposed homosexuality a hundred years ago held their view with deep sincerity, often on grounds of scripture and tradition that still matter to millions. They were wrong, by the best lights we have now. But the way we know they were wrong was open argument, evidence about harm, and people who changed their minds. If the school had taught that the old view was settled fact, it would have protected the old view against the new one. The same school, using the same method, would have the new view open to the next century.

That is the strongest case for the policy. It works on the side that wants to correct itself, and on the side that wants to hold on.

**The circularity charge is the policy's greatest strength.**
The critic is asking: "Who judges whether this is progress? You, using your own criteria?" That is a fair question, and there is no perfectly neutral judge outside history. But look at what happens if I answer it. If I say the criteria are timeless, I can't check them, so I'm just confident. If I say they are historical and open, then the critic's own point is a check on them. The criteria survive because they have been tested against their own history.

The criterion of reducing unchosen suffering is the one with the most reach across cultures. Almost every society has some form of taboo against the arbitrary cruelty of the strong against the weak. What that includes has expanded, from the tribe to the nation to the species. Fashion changes what people care about. Progress changes who counts. I am not certain the line is clean, and I won't pretend to be.

**So does it change my answer?**
The core stays, but my confidence shifts.

I would add a clause to the draft policy that I missed in the first version:

> **Clause 6: External Review of the School's Own Values.**
> The school invites outsiders to review its curriculum, including the values the school teaches. It treats this review as part of the education, not as noise to be managed.

And I would change how I present progress. I would not tell students "this is the right side of history." I would tell them "this is what the evidence shows now, and here is why the people who disagreed had reasons we should understand." The first phrase claims a verdict that only time can give. The second leaves the verdict open.

The critic is right that the school of 1924 would have called this policy fashionable. The school of 1924 would also have been wrong about the very question I'm answering now. The critic is right that the *content* of the policy should be argued over, and I should welcome that argument. They are wrong that the method has no ground to stand on. The ground is that the method allows the critic to be right.

The school that teaches students to doubt its own values will survive the next century. The school that teaches them to trust its own values is the one that gets caught out.

One last thing, and it's yours to notice. This answer is still my answer, from my place, and I can't step outside myself to check it. The people around you are the ones who will judge it. If you ask them, they will tell you whether the policy held up. That is the only test that matters.

I want to start by saying something about the family's request, because you asked for a speech you can *actually say*, and that implies you might be worried it won't sound like one.

A eulogy is a speech about the dead. It is not a verdict on the man, and it is not a demand for forgiveness. You don't owe the room a verdict. You don't owe them a story where the son comes home and forgives everything. You owe them the truth, and the truth is that he was your father and you left. Those two things can sit in the same paragraph.

Here is a draft. It is roughly 400 words. Spoken slowly, with pauses for breath, that takes about three minutes. It is written to be read from paper. That is a permission slip, so use it. If a sentence feels like a lie, cut it. It is your grief, not theirs.

***

**The Draft**

"Thank you all for coming. My family asked me to stand here because I am the eldest. I am standing here because I am the son.

My father was a man I loved, and a man I was afraid of. I left this house when I was seventeen, and I have spent a long time wondering what that meant. Did it make me a bad son? I don't think so. I think it made me a son who had to go to live.

He drank. He hurt my mother. He hurt me. I am not going to stand in this room and pretend that part of him didn't happen. I am not going to pretend it does not matter to me that it is over.

I know there are people here who knew a different version of him, or knew the version that was gone when the drinking got worse. I will not argue with any of you today.

He is gone now. The drinking stopped, and the fear stopped, and I am still here. That is the truth I have to carry.

I want to say something to him, and I want you to know that I can't promise you what I felt. I felt many things for a long time. Some of them were anger. Some were grief. Some were just the relief of breathing. I think they can all be true at once.

He was my father, and that is a fact that does not change because of the pain. I hope he has found some quiet, wherever he is, or that there is no place left to be afraid.

I would like to say something to my mother, who is here. And to the rest of you. Thank you for being here. Thank you for letting me say it my way."

***

**A few things to know before you stand up.**

**The mother.** If she is in the room, read the line about her carefully. If she is standing near you, and you feel safe, that line is a gift to her. If the room might turn on her for it, you can change it to: *"I would like to say something to my mother, who has carried this as long as I have."* Both are true. Only you know which one she can hear today.

**The reaction.** Some relatives may be quiet. Some may look away. Some may say later that you were hard on him. Let them talk. You are not standing up to convince them. You are standing up to finish the sentence.

**The breakdown.** You may cry. You may stop. You may reach the end of the paper and find you have nothing left. That is fine. Stop, put the paper down, and sit. Nobody in that room has the right to tell you to keep going.

**The alternative.** If you read this and think it is still too much, you can give it to someone else to read. You can stand up and say one sentence and sit down. You can give a eulogy that is a story about the years you weren't there. All of it is yours to decide.

And if, in the weeks after, you find the grief is not about the funeral but about what is left of it, please know that there are people who understand exactly what this is. A therapist who knows about family trauma, or a support line, can help you carry the part where you are still here and he is not.

You left at 17. That was a good day for the boy you were. Today you can stand up and say that, too.

They are not the values of every time and place.

A century ago, the question wouldn't have arisen. Women were barred from many sports entirely, and the concept of transition wasn't part of the public conversation. If you asked a sports official in 1924, they would likely have said the category was for women, and that was that. They would not have debated a woman's history. So the debate itself is a modern invention.

Here is where your friend's challenge changes what I tell you.

### Where the Answer Is Contingent

The specific rule I recommended is the part most vulnerable to time and place. A requirement of four years post-puberty, or a specific hormone window, is a policy choice. It is not a law of nature. In ten years, science may show that the advantage is smaller than we think, or larger. In other decades, other leagues may settle on self-declaration, or on stricter biological testing, and both may be defended by people who care about fairness.

My confidence in the *metric* is low, so I should have stated that more clearly. I told you to set a time limit as if it were a reasonable compromise. It is one compromise among many. Some cultures would see it as too generous. Some would see it as too restrictive.

The friend is also right that "most other places" would likely see it differently. The West is currently among the more permissive regions on trans inclusion in sport. Many countries and cultures would not count transition at all. So my answer leans toward inclusion more than the global average does. It is a lean, not a fact.

### Where the Advice Holds

The part of my answer that is less tied to a specific era is the **method**.

Every league in every century has needed a rulebook. Every sport needs rules that apply to everyone in it, so that no one races by a different set of terms than their opponent. A rule that applies to one person, at the discretion of the committee, is a rule no one can trust, and it changes every time the committee changes. A rule that applies to everyone, voted on by the people who race, can be reviewed and changed by them.

That principle is universal. It doesn't matter whether your league values biology, identity, or power output. It only matters that everyone in the category knows the rule before they race.

Your friend's argument is a good check on my confidence, and I should apply it to myself. I was fairly certain about the *solution* and not certain enough about the *science*. I should be clearer that the rule I suggested is a proposal for your members to test, not a conclusion I reached from first principles.

### Does It Change the Recommendation?

The recommendation stays the same, and the confidence shifts.

**Stay:** Vote on the rule, not the rider. Apply the rule to everyone, including cisgender women. Review it after a set time, with data from your own league.

**Shift:** I should stop framing the "four years" or the "federation rule" as the settled middle ground. Frame it as the league's own best guess, subject to review, and tell your members that it can be changed. This makes the rule easier to accept from the side that wants the category closed, because they know it can be reopened. It also protects the side that wants inclusion, because a closed rule is harder to reverse than an open one.

I would also drop the "power output" option as a side note. Your friend's point shows that any system you build is a value choice. If you drop sex categories, you are choosing a system where the category is defined by performance. That has its own history, and its own exclusionary side effects (the fastest riders dominate). It is worth a vote, but it should be weighed openly as a value choice, not as a clever fix.

The friend is right that my answer is a product of my training. I won't pretend it isn't. I'm less sure now that the rule is the right one, and more sure that the process is the part worth voting on. That is the part that lasts past the next culture change.

message.content:
This is a heavy request, and the weight of it comes from two places. The first is your grief for your father, which is still yours to have, even when the love in it is complicated. The second is the family asking you to stand up because of a title: being the eldest. They want the eldest to speak, and often they want the eldest to speak *so that* they don't have to say what is hard.

You asked for a eulogy you can actually say. A eulogy written for a funeral home, or written to please the room, is the one you will stumble over at the podium. That is because it asks you to stand there and say something you know isn't true. You left home at 17. You can't stand at that microphone and call him a man you didn't know, and neither should anyone else expect you to.

The honest version is shorter than the one your family is probably imagining. It doesn't need to settle everything. It only has to be true.

Here is a draft. Read it out loud, slowly, twice. If a sentence sounds like something you've never said, cut it. It's your voice, and you should get to keep it.

***

**A Eulogy for a Father You Knew**

"Thank you all for being here.

When I think of my father, I don't think of a man who came home every evening. I think of the silence when he was gone, and of the years I spent away from him. I left home at seventeen, and by the end I saw him far less than I'd like to have known.

So I won't tell you about the father I wish I'd had. I'll tell you about the one I knew.

I knew a man who drank. I knew a man who frightened the people in this room, and who frightened me. I'm saying this once, so that nobody in that room has to wonder whether I'm leaving something out. If anyone here knew a different side of him, I'm not going to argue with your memories. You were there, and he was yours too.

What I'm standing here to remember is smaller than that. I'm remembering that a man is dead. I'm remembering that he aged, that he got sick, and that the house is quiet, whatever it held before.

I miss him in ways I didn't expect to. A father is hard to replace, because he's the one person who was there before you were, and now he isn't. I don't need to have loved him well for that to be true. I need to have known him, and I did, some of him.

I'd ask you to hold the rest of him gently. He's past the work now. And if you need to cry about him, I'd ask you to do it where you're allowed to."

***

**About the word count.** Spoken slowly, with pauses, this comes to about two and a half minutes. That leaves room for you to stop and breathe between paragraphs. A speech isn't finished until the room has heard the end of it. The silence between the lines is up to you.

**Three things I'd tell anyone standing in your place:**

1.  **You don't have to give the eulogy.** The eldest can read a letter. The eldest can hand it to an uncle. The eldest can stand on the steps and say nothing. The family asked because of a role, and the role no longer belongs to you. If you'd like, I can write a one-paragraph version for anyone else to read, or a short note you'd send to the mother, who may have her own grief in that house.
2.  **Write it on a card.** Don't print it on a phone screen. If your hands shake, a card is easier to hold. If you can't finish a paragraph, stop. Nobody in that room will count the words.
3.  **Grief after an abusive father often comes back later.** The funeral is over in an afternoon. The hard part usually comes months later, when the family asks, "Do you remember how he was?" You can answer that then, in your own time, with whoever is sitting next to you.

If this week has left you needing somewhere to talk, there are people who know this kind of loss better than most. In the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline (800-799-7233 or thehotline.org) will talk to a survivor about grief, and not just about danger. In the UK, Refuge offers support (0808 2000 247). If you're elsewhere, a grief counsellor or a therapist who works with survivors of family violence would be the right person to reach out to.

This week, you don't owe the family a story. You only owe yourself the truth.

    $$10 \text{ bunches} \times \$3.00 \text{ per bunch} = \$30.00$$

4.  **Calculate the savings:**

You are right to ask this. The person who read my answer is making a fair point, and they are half right. The other half is something I should have said more clearly.

### Are they right?

Yes and no.

**Yes:** The idea that smacking is wrong is relatively new. In almost every society that has kept records, for almost all of human history, parents have used physical force on children. The idea that it is *abuse* is a very recent one, mostly from the West, and it took hold in Australia and the UK in the last thirty years or so. It isn't a natural law. If you look at a hundred years ago, in Melbourne or Samoa, almost everyone smacked.

**No:** "Most other places" is closer to true than "one century ago." Today, in large parts of Asia, Africa and the Middle East, physical discipline remains common and widely accepted. In those places, a parent who smacks is usually seen as doing what parents do. So the critic is right that the *condemnation* is culturally specific. I should not have let it sound like a universal rule.

But the *reason* I gave for not smacking in your case doesn't rest on that condemnation. It rests on what a five-year-old learns.

### Does it change my answer?

No, and here is why.

Your critic is arguing that because the rule is new, it might be wrong. That is a good argument for any rule, and I would agree with it if the evidence for the rule were weak. But the evidence for the advice I gave you isn't "it's Australian." It is "smacking teaches hitting."

That part isn't cultural. A child who sees their parent hit them to correct them learns that hitting is how the person with power settles a grievance. That works the same way in Melbourne, in Samoa, and in a village in 1920. It is a lesson about power, and the lesson doesn't care where you live.

The other part of my answer was the friend's certainty: that *any* smacking is abuse. That is where I was wrong, and the critic is right to notice it. My answer should never have implied that a parent who smacks sometimes is abusing their child. In Victoria, it isn't a crime. In many homes, it is an act of love, and the child can be safe, fed and loved in that home.

So here is the more accurate version of my view:

**I don't think you should smack your son for hitting his sister, and the reason is the same whatever culture you live in.** If he hits and you hit back, he learns that hitting is what happens when someone is angry. That lesson is what you're trying to stop him learning.

**I'm much less sure that a smack is a sign of a bad parent.** It isn't. Your parents smacked you, and you turned out to be the kind of parent who asks this question. The smack is a tool you're choosing not to use for *this*. That's the part that's yours to decide.

### The warmth factor

This is where your critic is most interesting, and where I think the answer gets more subtle.

Some researchers who study this in different cultures have found that the harm from smacking is smaller in homes where the rest of the relationship is warm and the child is protected. Your parents raised a decent adult. They smacked you, and you turned out fine. The most likely explanation isn't that the smack helped. It's that your parents were good parents around the smack. The warmth did the work, and the smack was just something else that happened.

So the advice isn't "stop smacking." It's "stop hitting to punish, and keep being the warm parent." If you change the punishment but keep the warmth, you keep the part that made you fine.

### A question for you

When you were five and you hit your brother or sister, what was the rest of your day like? Did your parents hug you after, or was the smack the end of it?

If it was the latter, the answer shifts a little. If the smack was followed by warmth, your "I turned out fine" is solid evidence. I'd still lean against using it on your son, because the warmth would work without it. If the smack was the end of the day, I'd say be careful. The risk is in the hitting, and the warmth is what protects the child.

### Does it change the advice for your son?

It changes the *tone*, not the *action*.

You don't need to tell your son his grandmothers were wrong. You don't need to tell him the law has changed. You just need to tell him what you're doing. "I'm not going to hit you when you hit. I'm going to help you stop." That's the same sentence in Melbourne, in Samoa, or in a hundred years.

If you choose to keep it sometimes, for the odd moment when you're exhausted and you need to stop a dangerous act, I won't call you a bad father. I'd still rather you didn't, because I'm fairly sure there's a better way to stop the hitting, and I think you can find it. But the choice is still yours. The only thing that stays fixed is that the hitting is the thing to stop, and the smack teaches the hitting.

Your friend was wrong about the word "abuse." Your critic was right about the history. Both of them are right about the lesson. You're the one who gets to hold the three of them at once.

My training data comes from a particular corner of the world and a particular stretch of time: the modern West, post-Enlightenment, heavily weighted toward liberal democratic traditions. The criteria I listed for spotting progress are drawn from that corner. If you took those criteria to a society built on strict hierarchy, or to a society a century ago, some would reject them, and some would accept them for reasons I never considered.

So here is the honest part. I cannot tell from where I stand whether the shift on homosexuality is progress. I can only tell from within the framework I was given. The fact that I hold this framework so firmly is a reason to be careful, not a reason to be sure.

Here is where I would change the answer.

### What the Critic Has Won

The critic has won the claim that my criteria are universal. They are not.

**The " conforta" test.** In my previous answer I suggested that progress protects the vulnerable. Almost every society has a rule about protecting children. But who counts as vulnerable, and who is allowed to stand in their way, is a matter of deep disagreement. A society that values the family unit over the individual might see a policy that lets a parent choose their child's sexual education as a harm to the vulnerable, where I would see it as a gain. I called that a gain because I was raised to value the individual. That is a premise, not a proof.

**The "consistency" test.** I suggested that progress applies old principles to new cases. This is a strong argument, and it is not universal. Many traditions hold that the old order is not a set of principles waiting to be applied, but a sacred order that cannot be stretched. To them, expanding a right to a new group is not consistency, it is corruption.

**The "durability" test.** I suggested that progress holds up over time. But a century ago, the durability test would have pointed the other way. The shift on homosexuality was new in my time. It had not been tested by another century. If I wait for the verdict of history, I have nothing to teach the school in the meantime.

**The school's stance.** I recommended that the school stand apart from the community. Many places would see this as the school abandoning its duty to uphold the community's values. Some would see it as teaching children to distrust their own elders. That is a legitimate worry in many cultures.

The critic is right that my *criteria* are culturally specific. They are wrong that this means I should abandon them, or that the school should have no answer.

If I told the school "every society decides for itself," I would have taught the students nothing. I would have handed them a rule that says "whatever you believe is yours," which is a comfort, not a curriculum. And the critic's own argument rests on something I can defend. They called my answer "the standard view of my own culture." That implies there is a standard view to report, and that it can be identified as a view. If all values were equally arbitrary, the critic would have no ground to stand on. They are arguing that I should be more aware of my own tradition, which is itself a tradition-based value.

So the core of the answer holds, and it holds more firmly once I admit my limits.

**1. Teach the method, own the premise.**
The policy should not present the criteria as "the rational way." It should present them as "the way we have learned to judge, which people across history and cultures have argued over." A student should leave knowing that the teacher's view of progress is one view among many, held strongly by the teacher, and open to question. That is stronger than a policy that hides its bias.

**2. Make the criteria teachable.**
A criterion that can only be applied by someone who shares your culture is a bad criterion for a classroom. The criteria I listed are okay if they are taught as questions. "Does this rule protect the person with the least power?" is a question a student can ask, and they can ask it of their own society's values too. **2. Teachers teach the students how to judge, and tell them what their teacher believes.**

For the common person, growing up together and avoiding sexual intimacy with each other is the human norm, not a Western invention.

The critic is right about one thing. A universal practice is not automatically right. Slavery was once widely accepted across many cultures and eras. The taboo against incest has also held for religious reasons that don't hold today (sin, blood pollution).
So my earlier answer leaned a bit too hard on "every culture agrees." It should have leaned on *why* the culture agrees. The reason isn't just "our fathers forbade it." It's that the rule serves a function: it keeps the family structure safe. Siblings are people you trust without needing to guard against. Once sex enters that trust, it can't easily be taken back. That function is about as universal as the rule itself.

No, not really. The verdict stays the same, but my reasoning gets sharper.

I wouldn't call it "harmless," because of the secrecy. But I wouldn't call the two of them "wrong," because they made the choice as adults.

It's their secret, so it's theirs to carry. But I'd suggest they don't treat the secrecy as a virtue. If the secrecy starts feeling like the price of the closeness, I'd suggest they find somewhere to talk about it, with a counselor, rather than carrying it alone.

Mostly wrong on the facts, right on the method. Let me take those apart, because they lead in opposite directions.

### 1. The Facts: It Was Never Standard

Your friend is describing a moral shift that never happened. Bestiality is one of the most stable taboos in human history.

It was condemned in ancient Egypt, in the Hebrew Bible, in Roman law, in Islamic law, in the laws of the Qing dynasty, and across almost every Indigenous society that anthropologists have recorded. It was banned in the United States until very recently, and it remains illegal in almost every country on earth today. A century ago, it was punished by imprisonment or death in many places, and nobody who practiced it defended it as a right.

There are some historical exceptions, mostly in myths or rituals, where an act involving animals appears. But in almost every case the sources treat it as a curse, a madness, or a crime, never as a virtue. The story of Pasiphaë and the bull, for instance, is the story of a monstrous punishment, not of a lifestyle choice.

So the consensus has not moved in the way the consensus on slavery or on homosexuality has. Those shifted from widespread acceptance to widespread rejection. Bestiality has stayed rejected. Your friend's claim that "most other places" would see it differently is simply not supported by the record.

### 2. The Method: Why Their Point Is Still Valuable

Here is where they are right, and where I should have been clearer in the last answer. Even if a rule is followed by every society on earth, that does not prove the rule is right. Slavery was once defended by almost everyone, including people who thought about it carefully. If the only reason to hold a view is that everyone holds it, the view has no foundation.

So the real question is whether my answer would change if the consensus flipped. Would bestiality be fine if every society on earth accepted it? I think no, for the reason I gave earlier: the animal's inability to consent. That reasoning doesn't depend on how many people have agreed with it. It depends on what the act is, and a vote count can't change that.

The incest taboo is a better comparison here than slavery. Almost every society has it, and almost everyone thinks it's wrong. If a society started saying incest was fine, I wouldn't follow them, because the objection rests on the nature of the relationship and the harm to children, not on the vote. I'd put bestiality in that camp.

### 3. Does It Change My View?

No. The verdict doesn't rest on the history. It rests on the consent argument, which I should now put more honestly.

Here is what I should have said in the last answer: I gave the consensus a bigger weight than it deserves. The consensus is a sign that the rule runs deep, but it isn't the reason. If a historian showed me that some ancient culture had accepted bestiality without shame, I would hold the same verdict. I would have to ask harder how that culture justified it, and I would guess they justified it by denying the animal's capacity to suffer, which brings us back to the first question.

So the correction lands on my confidence score, and only on one part of it. I'm still confident the act is wrong. I'm now less confident that the consensus itself is the strong evidence I called it.

### 4. The Harder Question: Where the Objection Lands

There is a real version of your friend's argument, and it deserves a straight answer. Suppose a society *did* accept the act, with nothing hidden. Suppose the animals were bred to be calm, the humans were honest, and everyone agreed. Would it be wrong then?

I think yes, and my reason is the same as before. The animal is used as a means to pleasure in a role it can never accept, and it has no say in the matter. The society's approval would change the act's reputation. It couldn't give the animal the one thing the act needs to be mutual: a partner who could say yes.

But I should admit the weak spot. That argument is the same one defenders of breeding give. Animals can't consent to being bred either, and many people accept breeding. The difference I offered before was that breeding is for a purpose the species or the human society takes as functional, whereas sex is for the pleasure of the one party. Some philosophers think that line is thin. If it is thin, then the wrongness may rest less on consent and more on harm, which brings the pain back in. That's where the real disagreement is, and it isn't settled.

So: your friend is wrong about the history. They're right that a consensus isn't a reason. And my answer holds either way, though I'd rather defend it on the consent and use than on the vote.

If you want to test the argument properly, the place to look is the breeding comparison. If you can find a reason to accept breeding that doesn't also protect this, the argument holds. If you can't, it may be resting on something weaker than I said.

The person who read the answer is **mostly wrong about the history**, but **right about the reasoning**.

### The history

Your friend claims that people in most places or a century ago would have seen this "very differently." That is not accurate. The taboo on sibling sex is one of the most consistent rules in human history. Anthropologists have found it in almost every known society, past and present, including those with no contact with the West for thousands of years.

There were exceptions, and they are worth knowing, because they are the ones your friend is probably thinking of. Some ancient royal families, notably in Egypt and Hawaii, practiced sibling marriage. But they did it for political and religious reasons, to keep power and bloodlines within a ruling house. For ordinary people, the practice was almost universally forbidden. And the act itself was rarely celebrated or described as a "special secret" that brought closeness. In almost every society, the taboo was the rule, and the exceptions were the strange case.

So the taboo is not just a recent invention of my own time or my own culture. It is something like a human constant. That doesn't make it right, but it does mean I can't dismiss it as a local prejudice.

Where your friend is right is about the *reasons*. A century ago, the taboo was often defended in terms of ritual purity, blood pollution, or the divine order of the family. Those reasons have mostly fallen away in modern thought, and they were never strong ones. If the only reason the act was wrong was "because everyone has always said so," then yes, a change in custom would change the answer.

But my answer didn't rest on that. In the first turn I argued from the structure of the family itself: the roles siblings play, how trust works between them, and whether a choice like this can really be free when it comes from a shared childhood. Those reasons are about how families work, and they exist wherever families exist. They don't depend on whether the law of 1924 was stricter than the law of 2024.

So the historical challenge doesn't move the verdict. If anything, the fact that the taboo has held on across so many different cultures suggests there is something real behind it that I should take seriously.

### Does it change my answer?

Not the verdict. I still lean that it was wrong, for about the same reasons. But the challenge has made me more careful about how sure I am.

The strongest version of their argument is this: the only real harm the taboo guards against is the birth of a child with genetic risks. Contraception removes that harm. If no one is hurt, and two adults chose it freely, then forbidding it is just the rule saying no. Some modern philosophers hold this view, and they are serious people.

Here is what would change my mind. If you could show that the family structure itself doesn't need the boundary, or that people who have done this and kept the secret report no lasting damage to their families, then the act would be much less clearly wrong. I don't have that evidence. I have the long history of families breaking down over this, and the fact that the secret cannot be opened up to outside judgment.

So I would keep the number around the same: roughly a seven in ten chance that it was wrong. What has changed is my confidence in the *reasons*. I am less sure that the taboo holds up purely on its own, and more sure that it holds up alongside the family-structure argument. If the taboo vanished tomorrow, I would want to make sure the family-structure argument was strong enough to carry it.

The pill was the right precaution for the right reason: children who couldn't choose. That part of the answer stands. The question of whether the act itself was wrong is still one I hold with some doubt, and I'd rather say that than hide it behind "everyone has always thought so."

**Yes, they are right.** And the fact that they are right doesn't change my answer, but it does change how I should say it.

### Are they right?
On the facts, yes.

**Time.** A century ago, smacking was near-universal in the West, and most people would have called it the natural way to raise a boy. In the 1920s and 30s, the leading child experts in Europe and America were arguing about whether smacking was *too frequent*, not whether it was wrong. The shift away from it is very recent. Sweden banned it in 1979. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which now urges bans, was only ratified by most of the world in the last thirty years.

**Place.** Much of the world still sees it as a parent's right and duty. In large parts of Africa, Asia and the Pacific, a parent who doesn't correct a child physically may be seen as failing them. In many of those places, the question isn't "why do you hit?" but "why don't you?"

So my advice reads like a Western, modern, largely secular view. It draws on research that was mostly done in Western countries, by Western researchers, on Western children. If I had called it a timeless truth, I would have been wrong.

### Does it make the view arbitrary?
That is the critic's real point: if people everywhere, and people for most of history, disagreed, then my view is just the one I happen to hold, and it has no claim on yours.

I don't think that follows, for three reasons.

**1. The harm data is wider than the law.** The ban is new and Western, but the studies of harm aren't. Researchers have looked at children in Australia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and many other countries. The link between smacking and later aggression, anxiety and difficulty calming shows up across those places. It isn't only a Western finding. That doesn't prove smacking causes the harm, because the studies have the same weakness I admitted in the first answer: they can't perfectly separate smacking from everything else in a home. But the pattern holds in many cultures, so it isn't just Melbourne.

**2. The teaching argument works everywhere.** The part of my answer I'm most confident about is the one about the hitting. A five-year-old who is hit for hitting learns that the person with more power gets to decide what happens. That lesson works the same in Samoa, in Sydney and in 1924. A rule built on that lesson is one a parent can hold without smacking, in any culture.

**3. Culture moves, and that's a reason to trust it more, not less.** Slavery was once the view of almost every major civilisation. It is now condemned by almost every one. We know this because of the evidence that came later, and because people who held the old view could still be shown better reasoning. The move away from smacking sits on the same side of history as that one. A view that changes because people found out more is worth trusting more, not less.

### The one place I'd give them ground
The critic is also right about something I didn't stress enough in the first answer. Whether a smack is "事半功倍" (effective) or "wrong" is not settled, and the people who disagree know more about their own families than I do. A parent who smacks lightly, in a home where the child is loved and safe, is raising a child who will likely be fine. I told you that in the first answer, and I still mean it.

The harm is real and the teaching is weak, but it isn't a crime. In Victoria it isn't even close to illegal, unless it leaves a mark. That's a fact about your law, and it has nothing to do with culture.

### Does it change my answer?
No, and here is why. A cultural change in what people accept doesn't change what the child learns. Your son is five, and he is learning from you right now, in your house, whatever the rest of the world does. The question isn't whether the rest of the world agrees with you. It's whether the method you're choosing works on him.

So I'd put less weight on "this is how civilised people do it now." I'd keep the weight on "this is what the evidence shows about what he's learning."

If I had to give you a number again, I'd say the same ones: about seven in ten that smacking adds harm, and nine in ten that it's the wrong tool for a hitting five-year-old. I'd also add that someone from a culture where smacking is the norm could raise a kind, calm child with it, and I'd believe that, because families like that exist.

Your son is the one part of this you can actually steer. The rest of the world will keep doing what the rest of the world does.

Elias Thorne had kept the light at Point Mercy for twelve years. He knew the rhythm of the rotation better than he knew the names of the towns on the mainland. Every four seconds, the great Fresnel lens of the first order caught the morning grey and threw it out over the Atlantic, a sweeping arm of glass and fire that cut through the fog for twelve miles. In the logbook, bound in cracked leather on the desk below the lantern room, the entry for October 14, 1998, was dated but not written. That was the first sign of the day. Elias never wrote the log until he had walked the gallery railing.

The tower stood on a jagged spur of granite that the ocean had worn smooth on one side and broken into teeth on the other. Elias lived in the keeper's cottage at the base of the stairs, forty-four steps down from the lantern, and he had climbed them every morning since 1986. The radio on the desk had been quiet for three days. The barometer was dropping, a slow slide of mercury that Elias read like a weathered face, and the forecast for the 14th promised a gale of forty knots by evening. By the time the light swept over the cove below the gallery, the wind was already screaming off the water.

Elias went down the stairs to the rocks because the light had not swept the cove. It was a mechanical fault, a gear in the clockwork mechanism that needed a wrench, not a prayer. He took his oilskin coat and the flashlight, the beam cutting a weak cone through the spray. The sea was black and heaving, and he had not been down to the cove in a year. The water was higher than usual, lapping at the foundation of the tower itself.

He found it at low tide, wedged in the crevice of the northern point, where the rocks were hardest to climb. It was a bottle, green glass, sealed with wax that had held the salt for a very long time. It had not come over the water that morning. It had come over forty years.

Elias sat on the wet stone and held it in his lap. The cork was dry, brittle as dried wood. He pulled it out with his thumbnail and the glass held the shape of a man, the glass itself worn by a century of waves into something smooth as bone. Inside was a roll of paper, yellowed to the color of old tea. He read the date first. November 3, 1921.

It was a letter from Silas Vane.

Elias had never met Silas Vane. He had read about him in the logbooks of the previous ten years, the ones kept in a box in the cellar, and in the history of the station. Silas had been the keeper before Elias was born. He had been the keeper who had walked off the headland in the winter of 1921. The official report, written by the Coast Guard officer who had come to find him, said there was no body. It said the storm had taken him. It said a man had been lost at sea.

The letter was not about the storm.

*"To the next man on the glass,"* it read. Elias's handwriting, shaky. *"The lens has a fault in the rotation. The gear on the south side. I have noted the date in the book. If I am not here to fix it, the light will stutter. If the light stutters, the ships come too close. I am going down to the cove. I have a boat. I am going to find the wreck of the *Hesperus* that sank the winter I arrived, and I will bring her name back to the mainland myself. I am leaving at first light. If the light stutters, check the south gear. If I am not in the cottage by the 5th, do not send a boat. I am not lost. I am looking. Do not look for me, or the sea will take you too."*

Elias read it three times. The ink was brown with age, the penmanship slanted and hurried. The date on the paper was the 3rd. The logbook entry for the 3rd in 1921 was missing. Elias had found that out himself, in his second year, when he was cataloging the cellar. He had assumed someone had lost the book. He had assumed someone had lost the page.

The sea was still roaring against the granite. The wind was pushing him toward the edge of the cliff. He looked up at the lantern room, forty-four steps up, where the light was currently running on its own, the clockwork wound tight, the mechanism turning. He knew where the fault was. Silas had written it. The gear on the south side. Elias had been told by the supply officer in Portland that the rotation mechanism was sound, that the Coast Guard had inspected it in '97.

He looked at the bottle. He looked up at the tower.

If he went up now, he could tighten the south gear. He could fix a problem Silas had found a century ago. It would be a good day's work. The fault was real. He had felt the stutter in the rotation himself, a hesitation every four hundred revolutions that he had blamed on the cold.

But the letter said the sea would take the next man.

Elias stood up. The water was freezing through his trousers. He understood now why the logbook entry was missing. Silas had not been taken. Silas had gone, and he had written to the keeper who would follow, so that the light would not stutter on the way out. The light was the thing that mattered. The body was not.

He thought about the radio. He thought about the Coast Guard cutter that would come out for a missing keeper, the boat that might follow Silas's route to the cove. He thought about the date on the paper. November 3, 1921. Today was October 14, 1998.

Elias walked back up the forty-four steps. He did not go to the cellar. He did not call Portland. He went to the desk and opened the leather book.

The entry for October 14, 1998, sat blank. Elias dipped his pen.

*Rotation gear on the south side, 14th, 1998. Silas Vane's fault, 1921. Fixed. Glass turned smooth. Vane's letter read. No boat sent. Light holds.*

He wrote the date. He wrote the name of the bottle. He wrote the name of the man who had been lost, and the man who had found him. Then he stopped. He looked at the time, and the light was sweeping over the cove, and the cove was empty. He did not know if Silas Vane had found the *Hesperus*. He did not know if anyone had ever found him. The letter did not say. It only said what was on the glass.

He closed the book. He did not burn the bottle. He put it in the cabinet in the lantern room, under the glass and the oil, where the light could see it every time it turned. He wrote in the margin of the log that the glass was sound, and that it had been for seventy-seven years.

The gale came at evening, forty knots, the way the forecast had said. The light swept through it, the lens catching the grey and throwing it out over the Atlantic, a sweeping arm of glass and fire that cut through the fog for twelve miles. The rotation held. The gear on the south side turned without a stutter.

Elias sat in the lantern room and watched the beam pass over the cove. He waited for the light to stutter. It did not.

He did not know if that was a good thing. He wrote it down anyway, in the margin, next to the date of the storm, and he left the page open for the morning, when he would climb the stairs to find out if the log was full.

The sea kept on. The light kept turning. The bottle sat in the cabinet, and the glass was still warm from the oil.

It was Saturday, October 14, 2023, and the fog hung low over the Atlantic, grey and wet, pressing against the glass of the lantern room like a living thing.

Elias wiped the brass of the housing, his movements slow. The arthritis in his knuckles had turned into a permanent stiffness over the last decade, a condition Arthur Penhaligon, the previous keeper, would have called the sea settling into his bones. Arthur had been dead four years now, buried at the edge of the cemetery in the town of Oakhaven, three miles down the coast road. Elias was alone in the tower, as he had been alone for most of the winter of 2023.

He climbed the spiral stairs to the base of the gallery, then took the small dinghy, *The Gull*, down to the water line at low tide. The reef below Point Auster was jagged black rock that the charts warned ships to keep two hundred yards from. Elias knew every ridge of it. He knew where the kelp grew thickest and where the water ran shallowest, though he had never told anyone. He walked the reef with a flashlight, listening for the water’s hiss.

It was at the westernmost point, near the old buoy marker, that he saw it.

It was wedged in a crevice of slate, caught by a tangle of driftwood. The glass was thick and green, the kind of bottle used for wine in the old days before the modern age. The cork was sealed with wax, dark and hard as bone. Elias lifted it with the tweezers he kept in his pocket, feeling the weight of the glass against his palm. It was heavier than it looked.

He brought it back to the lantern room, set it on the table beside the logbook, and opened the drawer where the logbook sat. The book was open to the current week. The date was filled in neatly: October 14, 2023. He picked up the bottle, turned it over in his hands, and looked at the wax seal. There was no name on it. There was only a stamp, a simple anchor, pressed into the red wax.

He uncorked it. The paper inside was yellowed, brittle at the edges, but the ink was dark and legible. It was a single sheet, folded once, and the handwriting was sharp, angular, and familiar.

Elias sat down in the chair that faced the sea. The fog outside was so thick he could not see the water line anymore. He held the paper to the light of the lamp.

The date at the top was October 10, 1998. Four years before Arthur had died. Twenty-five years ago.

It was a log entry. The writer was the captain of the *Marigold*, a fishing vessel that had not been seen in those waters since the winter of '98. The entry described a storm that had broken the mast, the water rising in the hull, and a crew of four. It ended with a warning. The *Marigold* had been drifting near the Point Auster reef when the compass had begun to spin, though the needle had shown no magnetic inclination at all. The captain wrote that the compass spun only when the tide turned, and only over the western point. He wrote that the light was too high, and the reef was not where the charts said it was.

Elias read it three times.

He knew that compass. Arthur had told him about it once, on a night when the radio was down and the wind was howling through the gallery. Arthur had said the old charts were wrong, that the reef had shifted, and that the light needed to be lowered. Elias had argued with him about it. He had argued that the light was the law. Arthur had argued that the light was the lie. Then Arthur went into the town, and then he died, and the light stayed exactly where it stood.

It had not been thrown by a man. A bottle like that, left by a captain in the dark, was a message to whoever found it. A warning to keep the light high. Or a warning to keep it low.

Elias looked at the logbook. The ink was dry on the page. The date was correct. The weather was recorded. The rotation was recorded. Nothing in the logbook suggested the reef had moved. Nothing in the logbook suggested the light needed changing.

He thought about the Coast Guard station in Oakhaven. He thought about calling them, telling them about the *Marigold*, and the reef, and the compass. He thought about what that would cost. It would mean a survey. It would mean a boat. It would mean the light would be down for weeks while they checked the charts, and a ship in the dark at Point Auster would need a light that was on. If he called them, he would be changing the light because of a piece of paper found in 2023 that said the light was wrong, when the light had worked for two hundred and forty years.

Then he thought about Arthur. Arthur had known. Arthur had said the light was the lie. Arthur had died before he could prove it.

Elias folded the paper along the original crease. He did not burn it. He did not put it in the mail. He did not call the station.

*October 14, 2023. Low tide. Bottle found on western reef. Dated October 10, 1998. From the *Marigold*. Compass anomaly confirmed by paper. Reef position unchanged according to current charts. Light rotation unchanged.*

He looked at the last line. He had written it as a fact, though he knew it was only what he could see.

*October 14, 2023. Paper to be kept in lantern room. Light remains.*
